history.dynasty: Satavahana-period origins; Reddy dynasty (12th century); renovated by Vasireddy Venkatadri Naidu (late 18th century)
history.period: Linga origins 1st-2nd century CE; present structure 12th century; major renovation 1796
history.summary: Amararama, one of the five Pancharama Kshetras of Andhra Pradesh, on the southern bank of the Krishna. Legend: the linga Tarakasura wore was broken into five pieces by Kumaraswamy on Vishnu's advice; one piece fell here and was installed by Indra, giving the town its name ('abode of the immortals'). The towering white-marble linga bears a red stain from a nail driven into it when it was believed to be growing. The complex holds three concentric circles of sub-shrines, Dravidian architecture with Buddhist stylistic influence, and inscriptions of the Kota chiefs and Vijayanagara emperors. Vasireddy Venkatadri Naidu (king of Chintapalli, later Dharanikota) shifted his seat to Amaravati in 1796 and rebuilt the temple, engaging nine archakas. Built-date conflict flagged: one source claims construction in the 12th century by the Reddys (Anavema Reddy), while another attributes the Chaturmukha linga to the 1st-2nd century Satavahana period; contributions of Chalukyas, Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara are also recorded.

name: Amaralingeswara Temple (Amareswara Temple)
town_description: Amaravati is a historic town in Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh, on the southern bank of the Krishna river. Once the Satavahana capital Dhanyakataka and a great Buddhist centre with one of South India's largest stupas, it is today a major Hindu pilgrimage town around the Amareswara Pancharama temple, close to the new Andhra Pradesh capital region.
